title: Judges
subtitle: No king in Israel
lead: Judges tells the story of Israel between the death of Joshua and the rise of the first kings. Its heroes are called shofetim, "judges," but most of them do not hold court: they are rescuers raised up in a crisis, leaders in war who then rule their tribes for a time. The book follows twelve of them, from Othniel to Samson, among them Deborah the prophet, Gideon and his fleece, Jephthah and his vow, and Samson and Delilah.

The book has a clear argument. Its opening chapters explain that Israel did not drive out the Canaanites and began to serve their gods, and they set out a cycle: Israel sins, God hands them to an oppressor, they cry out, God raises up a judge, the land has rest, and then they sin again, each time worse (2:11–19). The stories that follow show the cycle wearing down: the judges grow more flawed, women suffer more, and the tribes turn on each other.

The last chapters have no judge at all. A man makes his own idol, the tribe of Dan seizes a priest and a peaceful town, a Levite's concubine is raped and killed at Gibeah, and Israel nearly wipes out Benjamin. The book's refrain gives the diagnosis: "There was no king in Israel in those days. Everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes" (21:25).
facts: Not named. Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 14b–15a): Samuel. Most critical scholars: the Deuteronomistic writers of the 7th and 6th centuries BC, working with older tribal stories and poems.

Set between Joshua and Saul, about 1200–1050 BC on most historians' dating, or from about 1380 BC on the chronology of 1 Kings 6:1. The Song of Deborah (chapter 5) is often dated to the 12th century BC; the book as a whole probably reached its form in the late monarchy or exile.
The hill country of Canaan and the lands east of the Jordan, with battles in the Jezreel Valley, around Shechem, in Gilead and on the Philistine plain.
Hero stories, a victory poem, a fable, short lists of judges, and a closing set of stories about a lawless time, framed by a theological history.
Hebrew, with some very old poetry in chapter 5

audience.to: Israelites who lived after the time of the judges and knew what it was to have a king. The refrain "there was no king in Israel" (17:6; 21:25) looks back from the monarchy. Who they were depends on the view of authorship. On the traditional view, which names Samuel, they were Israel in the early days of Saul or David. On the critical view, they were Judah in the late monarchy and then the exiles in Babylon. These readers met the book as part of the history from Joshua to Kings.
audience.why: To explain why Israel fell apart after Joshua, and what kind of leader it needed. The book shows a cycle: Israel serves other gods, God hands it to oppressors, it cries out, God raises up a rescuer, and then it sinks lower than before (2:11–19). The judges grow more flawed, women suffer more, and the tribes end by turning on each other. Knowing the audience changes the reading. Under the kings, the book argues that Israel needs a faithful king and warns against kings like Abimelech. For exiles, it shows the same downward pull that later cost them the land, and it shows God still hearing his people's cry.
views: The Talmud names Samuel as author (Bavli Bava Batra 14b). The note that the Jebusites still lived in Jerusalem (1:21) fits a time before David took the city. The refrain about having no king fits a writer under Saul or early David, arguing for kingship.

Noth and most critical scholars see the book as part of a history written in Josiah's time or in the exile, using older hero stories from the northern tribes. The frame of sin and rescue uses Deuteronomy's language. Its readers were Judah after the fall of the north (18:30 mentions that exile) and the exiles in Babylon.

Brettler and others, such as Marvin Sweeney, read the book as political. Judah is given first place at the start and the end (1:2; 20:18). Benjamin, Saul's tribe, comes off badly, and so do Gibeah and Jabesh, the towns tied to Saul. On this view it argued for David's house against Saul's.
Webb, Amit and others read the book as carefully built, whatever its sources. It leads readers from Othniel's model rescue to the chaos of chapters 17–21, and asks what true leadership is.

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: the judges were real leaders in the two centuries or so between Joshua and Saul, and their stories happened as told, though some judges may have overlapped in different regions.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most academic scholars read Judges as old hero stories from separate tribes, framed by a Deuteronomistic editor with a repeating cycle of sin, oppression, crying out and rescue, and closed with chapters 17–21 that argue for kingship.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Many readers of every school follow the book's downward spiral: each judge is worse than the last, women fare worse and worse, and Israel ends up doing to its own tribe what it was meant to do to Canaan. The refrain 'Everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes' (17:6; 21:25) carries the argument.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Judges is one of the Former Prophets. The Talmud credits Samuel with writing it (Bava Batra 14b), and the rabbis weigh its heroes closely: Deborah the prophet, Gideon's ephod, Jephthah's rash vow, Samson the Nazirite who broke his vows.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Hebrews 11:32 lists Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah among the heroes of faith. Christian readers have seen the Spirit coming on the judges, the cycle of rescue, and the cry for a true king as pointing to Christ.

authorship: The Talmud says that "Samuel wrote his book, Judges and Ruth" (Bavli Bava Batra 14b). The refrain "there was no king in Israel" (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25) suggests a writer who lived after the monarchy began, and 1:21 says the Jebusites still lived in Jerusalem "until today," which points to a time before David took the city. Many traditional readers therefore date the book to the early years of Saul or David.

Martin Noth argued in 1943 that Deuteronomy through Kings is one history, written during the exile to explain Israel's fall. Judges' frame of sin, punishment and rescue (2:11–19; 3:7; 4:1; 6:1; 10:6) uses Deuteronomy's language. Wolfgang Richter traced an older "book of rescuers" (3:12–9:55) from the northern kingdom, later framed by Deuteronomistic editors. 18:30 says a priestly line served at Dan "until the day the land was taken into exile," which most scholars take as the Assyrian exile of the north (about 732–722 BC).

Many recent scholars, such as Barry Webb, Lillian Klein and Yairah Amit, read Judges as a carefully designed book whatever its sources, with a downward spiral from Othniel to Samson and a closing section that mirrors the opening. Marc Brettler argued that it is a political book, arguing for the kings of Judah against the house of Saul.

Plain English

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level, drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew and then checked verse by verse against other English versions, and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. YHWH is "the LORD," and Adonai YHWH is "Lord GOD" (6:22). Key terms are kept steady across the whole Bible: hesed is "loyal love" (1:24; 8:35); cherem is "under the ban" (1:17); yarash is "take possession of" a land or "drive out" a people; nachalah is "inheritance"; mas is "forced labor." The verb hoshia' is "rescue" and the judges are "rescuers." The book's refrain keeps the Hebrew image of the eyes: Israel did "what was evil in the eyes of the LORD," and in the end everyone did "whatever was right in his own eyes" (17:6; 21:25), as Moses had warned (Deuteronomy 12:8). The Song of Deborah (chapter 5) is set out in poetic lines. Where the Septuagint or a Dead Sea Scroll differs in a way that matters, the variant can be shown in place.

The two Greek texts

The Greek of Judges survives in two main forms, so different that Rahlfs printed both in full: the A text, close to Codex Alexandrinus, and the B text, close to Codex Vaticanus. Variants on this site name which Greek text is meant where they differ.

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible (2023), the King James Version (1611/1769), the American Standard Version (1901), Young's Literal Translation (1898) and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison.

The book has three parts. A double introduction (1:1–3:6): first the tribes' partial conquest and failures (chapter 1) and the angel's rebuke at Bochim (2:1–5); then Joshua's death, the new generation that did not know the LORD, and the cycle that will shape the book (2:6–3:6). The judges (3:7–16:31): Othniel (3:7–11), Ehud (3:12–30), Shamgar (3:31), Deborah and Barak (4–5), Gideon (6–8) and his son Abimelech (9), the minor judges Tola and Jair (10:1–5), Jephthah (10:6–12:7), Ibzan, Elon and Abdon (12:8–15), and Samson (13–16). A double ending (17–21): Micah's shrine and the Danite migration (17–18), and the outrage at Gibeah with the war against Benjamin (19–21), framed by the refrain that there was no king in Israel. Many scholars see the ending as a mirror of the beginning: the book opens with Israel united against Canaan, asking who should go up first (1:1), and ends with Israel asking the same question before a war against their own brothers, and getting the same answer, "Judah" (20:18).

Archaeology shows hundreds of small new villages in the central hills after about 1200 BC, which most historians link with early Israel. Canaanite cities in the valleys, such as Megiddo and Beth-shean, remained outside Israel's control for a long time, just as Judges 1 says. The Philistines settled the southern coast in the twelfth century, and Shechem was destroyed in the same period, as Judges 9 describes. Most scholars think the stories of the judges preserve memories of local tribal heroes, later gathered into a history of "all Israel." Traditional readers take the stories as accurate accounts, noting that several judges probably ruled at the same time in different regions, which explains why the book's numbers add up to more years than 1 Kings 6:1 allows.

Judges asks what kind of leader Israel needs. The first judges rescue Israel by the Spirit, by cunning and by courage. Then the questions start. Gideon refuses a crown but acts like a king; his son Abimelech takes one by murder, and Jotham's fable mocks him. Jephthah bargains his way into power and makes a vow that costs him his daughter. Samson is a Nazirite who breaks every part of his vow. In the last chapters, priests are for hire and the Levite who should teach the law causes a civil war. The refrain "there was no king in Israel" can be read as a call for a good king, such as David, or as a warning that the problem lies deeper, in a people where "Everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes" (21:25). The books of Samuel take up the question.

Few books of the Bible give more space to women, named and unnamed. They begin in strength: Achsah asks her father for springs and gets them (1:15); Deborah judges and prophesies; Jael kills Sisera; a woman at Thebez kills Abimelech with a millstone. As the book goes on their stories darken: Jephthah's daughter is offered up, or on some readings given to lifelong service, because of her father's vow, Samson's wife is burned, Delilah betrays him for money, the Levite's concubine is raped and dismembered, and the women of Jabesh-gilead and Shiloh are seized as wives. Many readers, from Phyllis Trible on, have seen the fate of women as the book's measure of Israel's decline.

spec.title: Judges as a book that undoes Joshua
spec.body: My own reading of the whole book: Judges takes the story of Joshua and runs it backward. Joshua opens with Israel crossing into the land and ends with the covenant at Shechem; Judges opens by repeating Joshua's death and moves to a king crowned at Shechem by murder (9:6). In Joshua the ban falls on Canaanite towns; in Judges it falls on an Israelite town, Jabesh-gilead (21:11). In Joshua all Israel fights Canaan; in Judges all Israel fights Benjamin (20). Rahab, the Canaanite woman, saves her family by hiding spies; at Bethel a Canaanite man saves his by betraying his town (1:22–26). I suggest the book is built to show the conquest unraveling from the inside: the Canaanization of Israel is the true subject. Scholars often note that Judges reverses Joshua's tone; the claim that it mirrors Joshua scene by scene is my own suggestion, offered for testing.

reading: Daniel I. Block, Judges, Ruth (New American Commentary, 1999)
A full evangelical commentary that reads the book as the "Canaanization" of Israel.
Barry G. Webb, The Book of Judges (NICOT, 2012)
A careful literary and theological reading by the scholar who made the book's design a central question.
A historical-critical commentary with strong use of archaeology and the Greek texts.
A detailed new translation and commentary, rich in ancient Near Eastern parallels.
A critical commentary attentive to oral tradition and the ethics of war.
Four studies of women in the Bible, two from Judges: Jephthah's daughter and the Levite's concubine.
Lillian R. Klein, The Triumph of Irony in the Book of Judges (1988)
A literary study of how irony shapes the book's verdict on its heroes.
Marc Zvi Brettler, The Book of Judges (Old Testament Readings, 2002)
A short critical study that reads Judges as political writing.
